title: Cross-language streaming + tool-call compatibility adapters and example patterns
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: deliver a cross-language compatibility layer and example patterns that make streaming responses, function/tool calls, and structured-output reassembly predictable and ergonomic across TypeScript, Python, and Go SDKs.

Scope:
- A lightweight compatibility adapter (polyfill) that backports newer streaming semantics (partial JSON emission, tool-call multiplexing, and incremental schema validation) to older SDK consumer codepaths.
- Language-specific shims: a TypeScript event-emitter helper, a Python iterator/async generator helper with rehydration utilities, and a Go channel-based stream adapter.
- Tool/function-calling ergonomics: utilities to coerce streamed partial arguments into typed structs/classes and a deterministic ordering policy when multiple tool responses arrive interleaved.
- Examples and recipes: 6 concise example snippets (two per language) showing: 1) streaming text + progressive JSON reassembly, 2) streaming-invoked function call with typed args and error handling.
- Migration guide: minimal code changes required for customers to opt into the new compatibility layer plus an incremental rollout plan for hosted clients.

Design decisions:
- We implement the polyfill as a very small surface: fromRawEventStream -> NormalizedInvocationStream. This normalizer emits a consistent set of events (token, json_patch, tool_call_start/tool_call_chunk/tool_call_end, done, error).
- Each SDK will expose an ergonomic wrapper on top of the normalizer: TS -> AsyncIterable of TypedChunks + EventEmitter helpers; Python -> async generator + `rehydrate_json` helper; Go -> Context-aware channel stream with Reassembler utils.
- For structured outputs we prefer progressive JSON patch approach (RFC-like patch chunks) to reduce re-parsing work and provide deterministic partial-state. The adapter exposes `applyPatch` helpers in each language.
- Function/tool call multiplexing policy: we assign deterministic stream IDs at normalizer time (derived from invocation metadata) and provide a `resolveToolCallSequence` strategy that prefers earliest-complete call and also exposes partial outputs for long-running tools.

Compatibility notes:
- The polyfill will detect older clients by user-agent SDK metadata; default behavior for old clients is pass-through with an opt-in call to `enableCompatibilityAdapter()` to avoid surprising changes.
- For performance-sensitive loops we provide a zero-copy pathway for TypeScript and Go, and a low-overhead parser for Python using incremental C-extension where available (fall back to pure-Python incremental parser).

Testing & QA:
- Unit tests for each language against a common test vector corpus (stream ordering permutations, interleaved tool chunks, malformed partial JSON).
- Integration tests gated on runtime-1.18 nightly that exercise the hosted streaming API under controlled latency and chunk-size distributions.
- Load test scenario: 10k simulated concurrent short-chat streams with 20% that trigger tool calls.

Rollout plan:
1) Merge language adapters behind feature flag in sdk-2.4.0-beta.
2) Publish example packages and guides; send to early-adopter list.
3) Enable opt-in toggle for hosted SDK clients; monitor errors and user feedback for two weeks.
4) Default enable after monitored stability window and security review.

Deliverables:
- TypeScript adapter + 2 examples + typings (src: sdk/ts/compatAdapter).
- Python adapter + 2 examples + migration guide (src: sdk/py/compat_adapter).
- Go adapter + 2 examples + sample server (src: sdk/go/compat).
- Confluence design doc and migration RFC.

Risks:
- Edge cases of incremental JSON reassembly leading to inconsistent schema states; mitigated by strong unit tests and a strict schema-acceptance gate that triggers a fallback to full JSON reparse.
- Performance overhead for tiny token streams; mitigated by opt-in and zero-copy fast-paths.

Notes for reviewers: please focus review on the normalizer event contract (events and guaranteed ordering), the typed-arg reconciliation approach, and the per-language ergonomic differences.
